title: NASA ScienceCasts: On the Cusp of Understanding
description: NASA is using sounding rockets to study the cusp, a point where the magnetic bubble that surrounds our planet dips inward and touches down to Earth.
keywords: NASA, ScienceCasts, SMD, Science Mission Directorate, Heliophysics, Cusp, magnetic field, sounding rockets, ionosphere, sun
via: the NASA Image and Video Library

Constantly shielding us from the Sunâs high energy particles is the Earthâs magnetic field.
Many imagine this field as a circle, slightly larger than our planet.
But, itâs actually shaped like this.
And near our north and south poles, there is a cusp â a point where two branches of a curve meet.
Itâs here that the magnetic bubble that surrounds us dips inward,
creating a funnel of magnetic lines that touch down to Earth.
This funnel allows the Sunâs high energy particles to race toward our planet and deposit themselves in our ionosphere,
80 to 800 kilometers above Earth.
We can even see the result - they create beautiful aurora, similar to the spectacular displays at night but on the dayside of Earth,
and only visible to the naked eye during the long polar night.
Now, scientists who want to learn more about effects of these particles are embarking on a special initiative
that is taking place from December 2018 to January 2020.
In a coordinated effort between multiple countries to understand the physics of the polar cusp,
scientists from NASA and the US, as well as from Japan, Norway, Canada and Great Britain have launched The Grand Challenge Initiative â Cusp,
a series of sounding rocket missions that will provide the data needed
to conduct nine unprecedented studies of near-Earth space at the polar regions.
This series will help scientists glean answers to a number of questions about the cusp.
Why is our atmosphere leaking out into space from the cusp?
How and why do the turbulent hot patches of dense plasma that exist inside the aurora region disrupt global communications?
What sustains strong updrafts of atmospheric gas in this region that can cause enhanced drag on our satellites as they orbit?
Doug Rowland, a space scientist at NASAâs Goddard Space Flight Center, explains:
âThe cusp is a great natural laboratory to understand how Earthâs atmosphere responds
to direct energy input from the solar wind. This kind of science can be done nowhere else on Earth.â

In some cases, launches will be conducted at nearly the same time from AndÃ¸ya and Svalbard,
providing simultaneous observations at different altitudes and latitudes.
Why use rockets instead of satellites or weather balloons?
Doug Rowland explains, âRockets are ideal for taking the measurements we need.
These rockets will be packed with monitoring instruments to capture information as they move upward in an arc,
and on the way down too. They can gather up to fifteen consecutive minutes of direct measurements from a specific region of space,
and you can launch them precisely. You want your rockets to fly right through the auroras just as theyâre going off.
Satellites cover a lot of area, but at high speeds they donât spend as much time making observations of any one location.
Balloons canât be launched high enough and their location canât be controlled as precisely as rockets.â
The new data gleaned from the Grand Challenge Initiative â Cusp will help scientists make better space weather forecasts,
and give us a better understanding of the particles responsible for one of the most breathtaking sights on our planet.
